catalog_quote: 36. I. Words susceptible of full stress take this on the first syllable, e.g. fairsingmenmnaige ‘magnanimity’. The stress is expiratory and very intense, as may be seen from the reduction of unstressed syllables (§§ 43, 106). It is this reduction that enables us to infer the position of the stress in Old Irish; further evidence is supplied by the pronunciation of the modern dialects, although in a few of these the stress has shifted in certain cases. The above rule holds for all simple words and for nominal compounds, including participles. 37. II. new_statements.quote: [p. 19, sec. 37] This change takes place in fixed compounds as well as in simple words and resulted from the position of the accent which fell primarily on the first syllable and secondarily on the third and fifth, e.g. dligthech, toimseo, ·tomnibther, for *dligethech, *tomesso, *to-monibither; similarly in loan-words, e.g. apstal, epscop, for apostolus, episcopus. [p. 74, sec. 124] There is no distinction between absolute and conjunct; the principal accent always falls on the first syllable except when the form contains an infixed pronoun. [p. xi] Prototonic = accented on the first syllable. Deuterotonic = accented on the second syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress at every word length, rule 10/100/1000..): agrees on primary stress on the first syllable. Adds detail: secondary stress on syllables 3 and 5, and the deuterotonic-verb exception (proclitic preverb outside the stress domain, so the accent is on the second syllable of the orthographic word), plus the syncope consequence of the pattern.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (the 'principal accent') falls on the first syllable of the word; O'Connell states this in passing (no dedicated accent section) as the cause of syncope: primary accent on the first syllable, secondary accent on the third and fifth syllables. The one systematic exception is the deuterotonic compound verb, where the first preverb (or a verbal particle carrying an infixed pronoun) is proclitic and the accent falls on the second syllable (the syllable after that preverb); when the same verb is prototonic (e.g. imperative, or after a conjunct particle) the accent is on the first syllable and the preverb is dropped or fused.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'secondarily on the third and fifth' syllables (p. 19, sec. 37), i.e. alternating secondary stress on odd syllables counted from the initial stress; used to explain syncope of the 2nd and 4th syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Deuterotonic verb forms are 'accented on the second syllable' (p. xi); in the imperative 'the principal accent always falls on the first syllable except when the form contains an infixed pronoun' (p. 74, sec. 124); verbs that always take a preposition appear only in conjunct flexion 'except in the imperative where the accent falls on the first syllable and the preposition is dropped' (p. 67, sec. 114); p. 7 sec. 7 notes that in the manuscripts words grouping about one principal accent are written as one word (clitic groups).
new_statements.identity_note: O'Connell describes the Old Irish of the Würzburg, Milan, St Gall and Turin glosses and the Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus (his 'third stage', roughly 5th-10th century), i.e. classical Old Irish, not a modern dialect; no variety issue.
